topics.title: Fantasy tales and the shape of a story

learn.hook: What would you paint if everything you painted came alive? A fantasy tale lets you imagine exactly that.
points: 'The Magic Brush of Dreams' is a fantasy tale about art, imagination and using a gift fairly.
Fantasy stories include things that cannot happen in real life: magic objects, magical powers, talking animals or imaginary worlds. Yet they often carry real lessons about good and bad choices.
Every story has a setting (where and when), characters (who), and a plot (what happens).
A plot usually moves through: exposition (introduction), conflict (the problem), rising action (things get harder), climax (the turning point), and resolution (how it ends).
The protagonist is the main character. The antagonist is the person or force that works against the protagonist.

example.q: Read this original tale: 'In a dry village of Bundelkhand, a boy named Kabir found an old paint pot. Whatever he painted for others came alive, but nothing he painted for himself ever moved. When the village well dried up, Kabir painted dark rain clouds across the sky, and rain poured down. A greedy trader demanded a painted mountain of gold, but Kabir refused and painted a garden for the children instead.' Think it through: name the conflict and one fantasy element.
steps: The problem in the village is that the well has dried up; a second conflict is the greedy trader's demand.
A fantasy element is something impossible in real life: paintings that come alive.
The resolution: Kabir uses his gift for others, not for greed.
example.answer: Conflict: the dried-up well (and the greedy trader). Fantasy element: paintings that come to life.

learn.reallife: Animated films, comics and many grandparents' bedtime stories use fantasy to make us think about real values like honesty and sharing.

games.title: Shape of a plot
games.prompt: Arrange the parts of a plot in order
items: Exposition: meet the characters and setting
Conflict: a problem appears
Rising action: things get harder
Climax: the turning point
Resolution: the problem is settled

games.title: About Kabir's tale
items: Kabir's paintings for himself came alive.
Only what he painted for others came alive.
The village well had dried up.
That was the problem that Kabir's rain clouds solved.
Paintings that come alive are a fantasy element.
This cannot happen in real life, so it belongs to fantasy.
Kabir painted a mountain of gold for the trader.
He refused and painted a garden for the children instead.
The greedy trader works against the hero, so he acts as an antagonist.
An antagonist is a character who opposes the protagonist.
The setting of a story tells us where and when it happens.
That is the meaning of setting.

quiz.q: Which of these is a fantasy element?
options: A boy goes to school by bus
A painted bird flies off the paper
quiz.explain: A painted bird cannot really fly, so it is fantasy. The others can happen in real life.
steps: Fantasy has things that cannot happen in real life.
A painted bird flying off the paper is impossible, so it is fantasy.
Answer: A painted bird flies off the paper
quiz.mistake: Thinks any interesting event is fantasy

quiz.q: Read: 'Whatever Kabir painted for others came alive, but nothing he painted for himself ever moved.' What does this suggest about the magic?
options: It works only for selfish wishes
It works only when used to help others
quiz.explain: The magic works for others, not for himself, so it rewards helping others.
steps: His paintings come alive for others but never for himself.
So the magic works only when used to help others.
Answer: It works only when used to help others
quiz.mistake: Misreads 'for others' and 'for himself'

quiz.q: In a plot, the turning point of greatest tension is called the ___.
quiz.explain: The climax is the turning point, after which the story moves towards its end.
steps: The plot rises to a turning point of greatest tension.
That point is the climax.
Answer: climax
quiz.mistake: Confuses the climax with the ending (resolution)

quiz.q: Who is the protagonist of a story?
quiz.explain: The protagonist is the central character. In Kabir's tale it is Kabir.
steps: The protagonist is the central character of a story.
In this tale it is Kabir.
Answer: The main character
quiz.mistake: Confuses protagonist with antagonist

quiz.q: Read: 'A greedy trader demanded a painted mountain of gold, but Kabir refused.' Why did Kabir refuse?
options: He did not want to use his gift for greed
quiz.explain: Kabir uses his gift to help, so he refuses a greedy demand. He paints for the children instead.
steps: Kabir uses his gift to help people, not for greed.
A painted mountain of gold for a greedy trader goes against that.
Answer: He did not want to use his gift for greed
quiz.mistake: Looks for a practical reason the passage never gives

quiz.q: Which part of the plot introduces the characters and the setting?
quiz.explain: The exposition comes first and sets up who, where and when.
steps: The plot begins by setting up who, where and when.
That opening part is the exposition.
Answer: Exposition
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order of plot parts

quiz.q: What is the setting of Kabir's tale?
quiz.explain: The tale opens in a dry village of Bundelkhand, so that is its setting.
steps: The setting is where and when the story happens.
The tale opens in a dry village of Bundelkhand.
Answer: A dry village of Bundelkhand
quiz.mistake: Does not look back at the opening sentence

quiz.q: Which word means 'the power to form pictures and ideas in the mind'?
quiz.explain: Imagination is the ability to picture things that are not in front of you.
steps: The power to picture things not in front of you is imagination.
Imitation, information and irritation mean other things.
Answer: imagination
quiz.mistake: Picks a word that starts the same way

teach.ask: Gappu flaps excitedly: Can a story with a magic brush teach anything real? What makes a story a fantasy?
teach.praise: Magic! Fantasy has impossible things like a magic brush, but it still has a plot and a real lesson inside.
teach.nudge: What kind of things happen in fantasy that can't happen in real life? Does it still teach a lesson?

revise.summary: 'The Magic Brush of Dreams' is a fantasy tale about art, imagination and using a gift fairly. Every story has a setting, characters and a plot that moves from exposition to resolution.
focus: Identify fantasy elements and the lesson they carry.
Name the parts of a plot in order.
Identify the protagonist, antagonist, setting and conflict.
remember: Plot: exposition (introduction), conflict (the problem), rising action, climax (the turning point), resolution (how it ends).
The protagonist is the main character; the antagonist works against the protagonist.
Setting (where and when), characters (who), plot (what happens).
traps: Don't confuse the climax with the resolution (ending).
Not every interesting event is fantasy; it must be impossible in real life.

topics.title: Art and justice: values, word families and Indian art

learn.hook: A brush can make a picture. Can it also make things fair? Let's explore the words of justice.
points: Justice means fairness: giving people what they rightly deserve. In stories, justice is done when the honest are helped and the greedy are stopped.
Word family: just (adjective) → justice (noun) → justly (adverb); unjust and injustice are the opposites.

Negative prefixes: un- (unfair, unkind), dis- (dishonest, disagree), in- (inactive, incorrect, injustice). im- is used before p, m or b (impossible, immature, imbalance), il- before l (illegal), ir- before r (irregular, irresponsible).
Indian folk and traditional art: Madhubani (Bihar), Warli (Maharashtra), Pattachitra (Odisha), Gond (Madhya Pradesh), Tanjore painting (Tamil Nadu), Phad (Rajasthan).
Art can speak for justice: artists paint, sing and write to show unfairness and to imagine a better world.

example.q: Think it through: Add the correct prefix to make the opposite of each word: legal, possible, responsible, honest.
steps: 'legal' starts with l, so use il-: illegal.
'possible' starts with p, so use im-: impossible.
'responsible' starts with r, so use ir-: irresponsible.
'honest' takes dis-: dishonest.

learn.reallife: Warli wall paintings show village life with simple shapes, and Madhubani art is painted on walls, paper and cloth. Both can be seen at state handicraft melas.

games.title: Which prefix makes the opposite?
items: possible
patient
mature
legal
logical
literate
regular
responsible
relevant

quiz.q: What is the noun form of 'just'?
quiz.explain: Just (adjective) → justice (noun). 'Justly' is an adverb and 'justify' is a verb.
steps: 'Just' is an adjective; we need the noun.
Just → justice ('justly' is an adverb, 'justify' a verb).
Answer: justice
quiz.mistake: Confuses the noun with the adverb or verb

quiz.q: Which is the correct opposite of 'legal'?
quiz.explain: Words beginning with 'l' usually take il-: illegal, illogical.
steps: Words beginning with 'l' usually take the prefix il-.
So the opposite of legal is illegal.
Answer: illegal
quiz.mistake: Uses un- or in- for every opposite

quiz.q: Which is the correct opposite of 'responsible'?
quiz.explain: Words beginning with 'r' usually take ir-: irresponsible, irregular.
steps: Words beginning with 'r' usually take the prefix ir-.
So the opposite of responsible is irresponsible.
Answer: irresponsible
quiz.mistake: Does not apply the ir- rule before 'r'

quiz.q: Madhubani painting comes from which state?
quiz.explain: Madhubani (Mithila) painting comes from the Mithila region of Bihar.
steps: Madhubani (Mithila) painting comes from the Mithila region.
Mithila is in Bihar.
Answer: Bihar
quiz.mistake: Guesses a state without recalling the art form

quiz.q: Warli painting, with its simple circles and triangles, comes from which state?
quiz.explain: Warli art is made by the Warli community of Maharashtra.
steps: Warli art is made by the Warli community.
The Warlis live in Maharashtra.
Answer: Maharashtra
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Warli with Pattachitra (Odisha)

quiz.q: Which word is the opposite of 'justice'?
quiz.explain: The opposite noun is 'injustice'. 'Unjust' is the opposite adjective.
steps: The opposite noun of 'justice' takes the prefix in-.
So: injustice ('unjust' is the opposite adjective).
Answer: injustice
quiz.mistake: Uses un- with the noun form

quiz.q: Which prefix makes the opposite of 'honest'?
quiz.explain: The opposite of honest is dishonest.
steps: The opposite of 'honest' is 'dishonest'.
So the prefix is dis-.
Answer: dis-
quiz.mistake: Guesses un- because it is the most common prefix

quiz.q: Which sentence shows justice in a story?
options: The greedy trader takes all the water.
The honest weaver is finally paid fairly for her work.
The thief escapes with the gold.
quiz.explain: Justice means fairness: the honest weaver gets what she deserves.
steps: Justice means fairness — people get what they deserve.
The honest weaver being paid fairly shows that.
Answer: The honest weaver is finally paid fairly for her work.
quiz.mistake: Does not link 'justice' with fairness

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: Why is it 'impossible' but 'illegal' and 'irregular'? And what does justice mean?
teach.praise: Brilliant! Justice is fairness, and the prefix changes to match the first letter: im- before p, il- before l, ir- before r!
teach.nudge: What does justice really mean? And which letter does each word start with, im-possible, il-legal, ir-regular?

revise.summary: Justice means fairness: giving people what they rightly deserve. We learn the 'just' word family, negative prefixes and traditional Indian art forms and their states.
focus: Know just → justice → justly, and unjust / injustice.
Match Indian art forms with their states.
remember: just (adjective) → justice (noun) → justly (adverb); opposites: unjust, injustice.
im- before p, m or b; il- before l; ir- before r; also un-, dis-, in-.
Madhubani (Bihar), Warli (Maharashtra), Pattachitra (Odisha), Gond (Madhya Pradesh), Tanjore (Tamil Nadu), Phad (Rajasthan).
traps: Don't use un- for every opposite: illegal, irresponsible, dishonest.
The opposite of the noun 'justice' is 'injustice', not 'unjustice'.
Don't mix up Warli (Maharashtra) with Pattachitra (Odisha).

learn.hook: Kabir's first painting was bright, his second was brighter, and his last was the brightest of all. Comparing is a painter's best tool!
points: Adjectives have three degrees: positive (bright), comparative (brighter, for two), superlative (brightest, for three or more). Use 'than' after a comparative and 'the' before a superlative.
Short adjectives add -er/-est: tall, taller, tallest. Double the last consonant after a single short vowel: big, bigger, biggest. Change -y to -i: pretty, prettier, prettiest.
Long adjectives use more/most: colourful, more colourful, most colourful.
Irregular forms: good-better-best, bad-worse-worst, many/much-more-most, little-less-least.
Equality uses as...as: 'This Warli painting is as detailed as that one.' Not as/so...as shows a difference.

example.q: Think it through: Fill in the blanks: 'Of all the paintings in the mela, Kabir's was the ___ (good). It was ___ (colourful) than the trader's poster.'
steps: 'Of all' compares more than two, so use the superlative of good: best.
'than' compares two things, so use the comparative.
'Colourful' is long, so use 'more': more colourful.

learn.reallife: Art competitions, cricket commentary and shopping all need comparisons: the best painting, a faster bowler, a cheaper kurta.

items.text: This mural is ___ than the one in the hall.
Meera is the ___ painter in our class.
The red is as bright ___ the orange.
This is the ___ colourful rangoli I have ever seen.

quiz.q: Choose the correct option: Kabir's painting is ___ than Ravi's.
quiz.explain: 'Than' compares two things, so we use the comparative 'brighter'. 'More brighter' doubles the comparison.
steps: 'Than' compares two things.
Use the comparative: brighter ('more brighter' doubles it).
Answer: brighter
quiz.mistake: Uses 'more' and '-er' together

quiz.q: What is the superlative of 'good'?
quiz.explain: 'Good' is irregular: good-better-best.
steps: 'Good' is irregular: good – better – best.
The superlative is best.
Answer: best
quiz.mistake: Adds -est to an irregular adjective

quiz.q: Which is correct?
quiz.explain: Long adjectives form the superlative with 'the most'.
steps: Long adjectives like 'beautiful' form the superlative with 'the most'.
So: the most beautiful.
Answer: the most beautiful
quiz.mistake: Adds -est to a long adjective

quiz.q: What is the comparative of 'bad'?
quiz.explain: 'Bad' is irregular: bad-worse-worst. 'Worse' compares two things.
steps: 'Bad' is irregular: bad – worse – worst.
The comparative is worse.
Answer: worse
quiz.mistake: Confuses worse (comparative) with worst (superlative)

quiz.q: Choose the correct spelling of the superlative of 'happy'.
quiz.explain: Change -y to -i and add -est: happiest.
steps: For adjectives ending in -y, change y to i and add -est.
happy → happiest.
Answer: happiest
quiz.mistake: Does not change the 'y' to 'i'

quiz.q: Which sentence uses the comparative degree?
options: Asha's drawing is neater than mine.
quiz.explain: 'Neater than' compares two drawings. 'The neatest' is superlative.
steps: The comparative compares two things, often with 'than'.
'Asha's drawing is neater than mine' is comparative.
Answer: Asha's drawing is neater than mine.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up comparative and superlative

quiz.q: Choose the correct option: 'Of the three brothers, Raju is the ___.'
quiz.explain: With three or more, use the superlative: the tallest.
steps: There are three brothers — more than two.
With three or more, use the superlative: the tallest.
Answer: tallest
quiz.mistake: Uses the comparative for more than two

quiz.q: What is the comparative of 'big'?
quiz.explain: After a single short vowel, double the last consonant: big → bigger.
steps: 'Big' has a single short vowel before one consonant.
Double the last consonant: big → bigger.
Answer: bigger
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the final consonant

teach.ask: Gappu painted three worms. How do I compare them? When do I say 'longer' and when 'longest'?
teach.praise: Wonderful! 'Longer than' compares two, 'the longest' compares three or more, and long words use 'more' and 'most'!
teach.nudge: How many worms are we comparing when we use 'longer'? And when we use 'longest'?

revise.summary: Adjectives have three degrees: positive, comparative (for two, with 'than') and superlative (for three or more, with 'the'). Short adjectives add -er/-est, long ones use more/most, and some are irregular.
focus: Choose comparative or superlative from the sentence.
Apply spelling rules: doubling and -y to -i.
remember: Short: tall, taller, tallest; big, bigger, biggest; pretty, prettier, prettiest.
Long: colourful, more colourful, most colourful.
Equality uses as...as; not as/so...as shows a difference.
traps: Don't use 'more' and '-er' together: 'brighter', not 'more brighter'.
Don't add -est to a long adjective: 'the most beautiful'.
